INTRODUCTION 
 
 
 
 I,  the Chairman of  the Standing Committee on Railways (2004-
05), having been authorised by the Co mmittee to present the Report on 
their behalf, present this Ninth Report of the Standing Committee on 
Railways (2004-05) on ‘The Railways (Amendment) Bill, 2004’. 
 
2. The Railways (Amendment) Bill, 2004 was introduced in Rajya Sabha on 20 th 
December, 2004 and referred to the St anding Committee on Railways for 
examination and Report. They t ook evidence of the represent atives of the Ministry of 
Railways on  7th and 17th  February, 2005 and Ministry of Law & Justice on 28 th April, 
2005.  
 
3. The Committee considered and adopted the Report at their sitting held on  10th 
May, 2005. Minutes of the sittings held on 7 th and 17th  February, 28 th April and 10 th 
May, 2005 form Part-II of the Report.  
 
4. The Committee wish to express their thank s to the officers of the Ministry of 
Railways (Railway Board) and t he Ministry of Law & Justice for appearing before the 
Committee and furnishing the material and information which the Committee desired 
in connection with the examination of the Railways (Amendment) Bill, 2004 and 
sharing with them the issues concerning the subject which came up for discussion 
during evidence.

REPORT 
CHAPTER I 
 
THE RAILWAYS (AMENDMENT) BILL, 2004 – AN INTRODUCTION 
 
 Indian Railways owns 4.23 lakh hectares of   land, out of which 3.19 lakh hectares i.e. 
75.2% of the total land holding is  used for Railway operations su ch as track and structures 
including colonies and stations.  Approximately 10.14% (43,000 hectares) of the total land are 
vacant land  and 0.47% (2240 hectares) of land is under encroachment.   Substantial part of 
vacant land have prima-facie potential for devel opment.   It was envisaged in Ninth Plan 
document that there is a need for additional resources from non-tariff measures.  The Planning 
Commission had also emphasised commercial utilization of vacant Railway land and the 
space above such land to supplement the internal  revenues of the Railways.  Accordingly, the 
Indian Railways have started the process of identification, planning and  commercial 
development of railway land in 2001-02  to boost their non- traditional revenues.  So far the 
Railways have identified 61 major sites having co mmercial potential and started carrying out 
market feasibility studies.  Out of 61 sites earmarked by the Railways, 9 sites have been 
finalised with an expected revenue of  Rs.21 crore and bids for 17 sites having potential of Rs. 
110 crore are under process.  However, bids for 24 sites were cancelled/dropped on account of 
a number of reasons, for example, the land was not free from all encumbrances or 
encroachment and the parties did not come forward.    The feasibility study is still in progress 
for the remaining 11 sites. 
 
1.2 During the oral evidence, the Chairman, Railway Board apprised the Committee as 
under:- 
“Besides these 61 major sites, we have 54 smaller sites each  having  an area 
less than 1000 sq. meters  being tackled at the Zonal Railway level.” 
 
1.3  However, Railways have not been able  to materialize earnings through property 
development  up to the desired level despite the existence of separate land management cell in 
each zone on account of the following constraints:- 
(i) the primary mandate of the Railways is to carry goods and passengers and the 
property development becomes the secondary function of the Railways; 
(ii) property development  is a very se nsitive to market forces which requires 
expertise in real estate management; 

 8
(iii) the Railways not having any expertise in  real estate development as a full time 
activity; 
(iv) resistance by the State Govt. to cha nge in land use by the Railways other than 
operation of trains; 
(v) non-clearance of development scheme s on railway land/building by local 
authorities; 
(vi) absence of clear cut provision in  the Railway Act, 1989 for commercial 
utilisation/development of Railway land. 
 
1.4 Emphasizing the need for cr eation of a full time agency like Rail Land Development 
Authority to look after the commercial utilis ation of vacant land, the Chairman, Railway 
Board submitted before the Committee as under:- 
“We have got 43,000 hectares of vacant land.  Our purpose is that wherever 
there is a vacant land, we should be able to commercially exploit the same.  
But it needs a dedicated organization.  The primary function of our engineering 
department is entirely different.  Th ey could not spare much time for this 
nature of work, which needs a whole-time attention.  Secondly, we are not 
experts in the field of pr operty development.  We need expertise.  That was 
one of the reasons.  As regards legal pr ovisions, there is no specific provision 
in the Railways Act, wherein we may go in  for commercial utilization of land.  
There is also the diffidence on the part of the State Government.  They are the 
main impediments because of which th e Indian Railways could not proceed 
further.” 
 
1.5   To overcome the same, the Ministry of Ra ilways went to Cabinet  to get the mandate 
to develop  the vacant land for commercial purpos e and got the approval of the  latter on 8 th 
December, 2004. Accordingly, the Ministry of Railways introduced ‘The Railways 
(Amendment) Bill, 2004’ in Rajya Sabha on 20th December, 2004 during the Third Session of 
Parliament (14th Lok Sabha).    
 
1.6 The proposed Bill envisages amendment to  the existing Railway Act, 1989 with a 
view to providing (i) the constitutional manda te to develop the vacant land for commercial 
purpose and (ii) establishing a Rail Land Deve lopment Authority (RLDA) to  take over 
exclusively the development of vacant lands and space above such lands.  The Bill in question 

 9
has 4 Clauses. Clause-1 deals with its short title and commencement Clause-2 deals with 
Amendment of Section 2 of the Railways Act,  1989 (Chapter-I, Definitions), Clause-3 deals 
with the insertion of a new Chapter IIA in the Railways Act, 1989 and Clause 4 deals with 
Amendment of Section 11 (Chapter-IV, Construction and Maintenance of Works) of the 1989 
Act.  The proposed Chapter II A incorporates the provision for establishment of Rail Land 
Development Authority, its composition, terms a nd conditions of appointment of the office 
bearers, functions of Authority,  powers of  the Authority, procedure of transaction of 
business, appointment of officers and employees and their salaries and power of Authority to 
make regulations.  
 
1.7 In the statement of objects and reasons of  the Bill, the Ministry of Railways have 
stated that the development of  property being a specialised fi eld it requires expertise, 
marketing acumen, innovative strategies and fu ll time devotion.  Against this backdrop,  the 
Ministry considered it necessary to set up  a separate authority to be called  the Rail Land 
Development Authority under th e Railways Act, 1989 which woul d exclusively deal with 
commercial development of railway land and air space above such land.  It is also proposed to 
amend Section 11 of the Railways Act so as to include commercial utilisation of railway land 
as part of the work of the Railways. 
 
1.8   The proposed Authority will focus on deve loping only those vacant land which have 
potential for commercial development.  The Mi nistry have assured th e Committee that only 
those vacant lands which are not required atleast for next 15-20 years for rail operations 
would be considered for commercial purposes.  The RLDA would also assist the Railway for 
certification of land plans from Revenues Authorities.     
 
1.9 The Railways will utilise the earnings re alized from commercial development of 
Railway Land for various developmental works es pecially passenger amenities for the benefit 
of  rail users. 
 
1.10 According to the Ministry of Railways the thrust of the commercial development 
would be as follows:   
(a) To generate revenue from non-traditional source. 
(b) To beautify the station  surroundings and improve the general ambience and 
aesthetics through commercial use of idle space; 

 10
(c) To provide modern amenities to the rail user; 
(d) To reduce traffic congestion in the st ation circulating areas by remodeling of  
station buildings and adjoin ing space thereby facilita ting efficient  passenger 
handling and improving customer satisfaction; 
(e) To check/prevent encroachments in the prime land by putting the land to 
commercial use.  The authority woul d liaison with State Government for 
expeditious eviction of encroachme nt by the railway on land to be 
commercially utilised.  

 11
   
CHAPTER – II 
 
RAIL LAND DEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY 
 
 
2.1 Till now Engineering Department of th e Railways has been in-charge of land 
management and deals with commercial usages  of vacant lands.  The Department took up 
property development in the year 2001 as commercial use of land.   However, due to certain 
constraints as mentioned in the precedi ng Chapter, sufficient confidence among the 
investors/developers could not be generated and as a result no substantial headway could be 
made. Property development is a specialised field  which needs full time attention and calls 
for flexibility to mould strategies in tune w ith the hyper sensitive real estate market.  
Railways, being primarily involved in the core business of traffic cann ot have the requisite 
flexibility to respond quickly to  the varying demands of real estate market.  Moreover, the 
property development schemes/plans require ap proval of the local/sta tuory bodies,  which 
require close interaction  with  such bodies.  Against this back ground, the Ministry of 
Railways have desired to go for creation of  an exclusive body to be called, Rail Land 
Development Authority (RLDA) which can take care of devel opment of vacant rail land on 
full time basis.  The Engineering Department of the Railways will deal with all matters except  
the property development.   
 
Definition  
2.2 In the Bill a new clause 32A is proposed to  be inserted in Section 2 of the Railways 
Act, 1989 defining the Railway Land as under:-  
 
“railway land’ means any railway land other than falling under railway       
  track;”     
 
2.3 On being pointed out that it has not been properly defined.  The representative of the 
Department of Legal Affairs, Ministry of  Law & Justice stated:- 
“Clause 31 of Section 2 is  related to the definition clause.  There are various 
definitions.  Railway land has not been defined but the definition of the word ‘railway’ 
includes land also…. as all lands within the fences or other boundary marks indicating 
limits of the land appurtenant to a railway.  Railway includes a land also which is 
within the boundary of the railway.” 

 12
 
2.4 When  further enquired whether there is any need for a separate  definition of railway 
land in the Bill whereas the same has been defi ned in the clause 31(a) of The Railways Act, 
1989, the representative of the Ministry of Law & Justice stated:- 
“In the light of the object of this Bill as to whether it needs a special definition.  
Railways must have expressed the desire th at Railways should be clearly defined and 
therefore the Legislative Department has pr ovided this particular formulation of the 
railway land.  But if this Committee wants that  it is not sufficient and I also feel that 
the word ‘railway land’ has not been defined.  So, in the definition itself, you are using 
the word ‘railway land’.  Then it is subject to improvement…. We can use it with 
better formulation as given in clause 32(a) in consultation with legislative Department 
in the light of the purpose for which this Act is being passed.”  
  
Functions 
2.5 The RLDA  will focus on generation of  non-tariff resources through commercial 
development of vacant lands.  The Authority w ould gradually acquire the required expertise 
and start providing consultancy later on.  The ma in functions of the Authority as per the 
Clause 4D of the proposed Bill would be as under:- 
(1) The Authority shall discharge such f unctions and exercise such powers of the 
Central Government or a railway admini stration in relation to the development 
of railway land and as are specifica lly assigned to it  by the Central 
Government. 
(2) In particular, and without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing power, 
the Central Government may assign to the Authority all or any of the following 
functions, namely:- 
(i) to prepare scheme or scheme s for use of railway land in 
conformity with the provisions of this Act; 
(ii) to develop railway land for co mmercial use as may be entrusted 
by the Central Government or a railway administration for the 
purpose of generating  revenue by non-tariff measures; 
(iii) to develop and provide c onsultancy for construction or 
management services and undertake operation in India in 
relation  to the development of land and property; 

 13
(iv) to carry out any other work or function as may be entrusted to it 
by the Central Government, or a railway administration by 
order in writing. 
 
Composition 
2.6. As per the Bill, RLDA would be set up w ith skeleton  staff.  Its composition as 
incorporated in clause 4Bof the Bill would be as follows:- 
     (1) The Authority shall consist of a Chairman, Vice-Chairman and not more than 
four members including experts from out side the railway administration. 
     (2) The Member Engineering, Railway Board shall be the Chairman, ex-officio of 
the Authority. 
     (3) The Vice-Chairman and the other members shall be appointed by the Central 
Government and shall be chosen from amongst persons who are or have been 
working in the Civil Engineering, Finan ce and Traffic discip lines of a railway 
administration and having adequate experience in the relevant discipline as the 
Central Government may consider necessary.  
 
2.7 Regarding the Composition, the Chairman, Ra ilway Board further explained the same 
during the course of evidence as under:- 
“Member Engineering will be Ex-Officio Chai rman.  He will be assisted by the Vice-
Chairman and four members.  Out of these four members, three will be from the 
discipline of civil engi neering, traffic and finance.  The fourth member would be an 
expert from outside having expe rtise in real estate planni ng and development.  Their 
job specification, job require ment, qualification etc. will be spelt out; the Authority 
will create the rules and regulations” 
  
2.8 Advice of each Member will be given equal weightage and decisions  would be taken 
in the Board meetings as per th e rules and regulations to be fr amed later. However, normally 
these decisions would be taken by consensus as a rule and by majority as an exception.     
Chief Executive of the Authority would be the Vice Chairman who will be a technocrat 
having wide experience in land management, construction of building and real estate. 
 

 14
Administrative expenditure 
2.9  According to the Ministry the expenditure on establishment will be insignificant as 
compared to earnings.  The Financial Memorandum attached with the Bill states that the 
recurring expenditure of the Authority is  estimated to be Rs.75 lakhs per annum 
approximately which will be defrayed out of the Consolidated Fund of India.       
 
Modus Operandi 
2.10 The working of the proposed Rail Land Development Authority will be as under:- 
(i) Potential sites for commercial utiliza tion shall be identified either by Railway 
or by the Authority itself.  If specific  land is not required for operational 
purposes/future expansion, then the site will be given to RLDA for commercial 
development. 
(ii) RLDA will carry out necessary market survey to assess the potential and work 
out the best mode of commercial development from the angle of revenue 
returns and accordingly proceed with the bidding process. 
(iii) Developer will be finalized through tr ansparent open bidding process.  All the 
earnings realized will go to Railways.  
(iv) An agreement for development will be executed between RLDA (on behalf of 
Ministry of Railways) and the developer.  Lease agreement  for the developed 
property will be executed between Railw ays (the owner of the land) and the 
developer. 
 
2.11 Above activities are proposed to be executed by RLDA opera ting from Delhi.  This is 
possible as the role of the Railway, after identification and handing over the site to RLDA, is 
minimal till the development plans for the commercial use of the site are made and such stage 
would come only after finalizati on of bids and entrusting  the site to the developer.  For 
execution of the commercial project, developer will be entirely responsible for doing the job 
as per the local building by – laws and laid down specifications.  Such project cannot be put to 
use without clearance of local authorities, who are required to be satisfied whether the project 
conforms to the laid down guideline, the devel oper will ensure total compliance.  Apart from 
this, RLDA, at that stage may also engage cont ract supervisors for ove rseeing the project(s).  
Depending upon the volume of work load, RLDA may appoint field coordinating officers 
who will liaison with various Zonal Railways and the concerned States in regard to 
commercial development falling in that region. 

 15
 
Land Lease 
2.12 The terms and conditions of l ease would be the same as one being followed at present.  
Presently, commercial devel opment on railway land is being done as per draft lease 
agreement vetted by Ministry of Law & Justic e.  As per this, land can be leased for 
commercial development upto 60 years extendable  upto 90 years. To get back the leased 
land by the Railways for its urgent operational requirement in midway of lease period,  
necessary premature termination clause has been kept in the lease agreement as under:- 
“In case the lessor needs th e space so leased to the lessee at any time prior to 
the expiry of the lease period, the lessor reserves  the right to acquire 
possession of the premises after giving one hundred and eighty days notice to 
this effect to the lessee.  On such premature termination of the lease due to 
lessor’s requirement, the lessee shall be entitled for compensation equivalent  
to the proportionate premium for the unexpired period of the lease together 
with simple interest @ 12%.” 
  
2.13 Lease period is normally kept longer fo r major sites where developers investment 
would be substantial.  Howeve r, only such Railway land parc els which are not required in 
foreseeable future, would be taken up for comm ercial development subject to its market 
potential.  For  commercial development of built-up space, lease period would be much 
shorter. 
 
2.14 Clarifying whether the land leased to the Railways by the State Governments can be 
further leased to the developers, the represen tative of the Department of Legal Affairs, 
Ministry of Law & Justice submitted as under: 
“The State Governments must have allotted that land through a lease deed or a lease 
agreement.  If in that lease agreement th ere was a condition that you cannot divert the 
use of this land for any other purpose, then  the party who has been granted that land 
by the State Government will have to surr ender the excess land  or whatever land.  
They cannot sell it to any other party because they have got a limited right over it.  So, 
it is a question of fact …  If there is a condition in the agreement of sale or lease by 
which the lease has been allo tted to the Railways, then they (Railways) will be bound 
by those terms and conditions.” 

 16
 
CHAPTER – III 
 
RAILWAY LAND USAGE,  MANAGEMENT AND ENCROACHMENT 
 
Land Usage 
3.1  Over the years, the Railways have ac quired 4.23 lakh hectare of land  for their 
primary mandate of operations of trains. Some of  these lands have been provided free of cost 
by the State Governments or on no minal charges and rest of the lands have been acquired for 
the Railways by State Governments from the ge neral public for public purposes after paying 
compensation.  Some of the lands are still on long term lease to the Railways.  The Railways 
have taken these lands for public purpose  i.e.  rail carriage.  The Ra ilways are the owner as 
well as the lessee of the lands available with  them.  The Engineering Department in the 
Railways  are the custodian of the lands availabl e with the Railways.  At present there is no 
legal provision in the existing Railway Act, 1989 to develop the rail land for the purpose other 
than the operation of trains.   
 
3.2. Elaborating on the need to change the land usage of the vacant land for commercial 
purposes, the Chairman Railway Board stated as under:- 
“We get the land for the public usage…. We have taken lands from State 
Governments.  We have got the Government land also.  The State Government can say 
that once you have changed the land use and it is not required by the Railways, then 
you have to return it back.  It is a very valid problem which we have been facing….the 
relevant part, which we are going to am end is Chapter IV in Section 11 of the 
Principle Act – The Railway Act (1989).  In Section 11 of the Pr inciple Act, after 
Clause (d), the following clause shall be inserted, ‘(da) developing any Railway land 
for commercial use’.   This is the main part.  When we get powers under the Railway 
Act, then it can supersede all the provisions of the Stat e Governments.  When this 
Railway Act comes into force and it has been effected, nothing can supersede it so far 
as public carriage is concerned.” 

 17
 
3.3. Responding to a query of the Committee whether the commercial utilisation of surplus 
railway land can be encompassed within the ‘public purpose’, the re presentative of the 
Ministry of Law & Justice elaborated as under:- 
“It can be a public purpose.  But it all de pends on the facts of the case……  If the 
Railways have got some land a nd if they propose to put up  a commercial complex to 
give some facilities to the railway travelle rs and  the persons living in that  area, it 
would come within the use of public because it is going to give facility for the use of 
public.   Then, they will earn revenue also, which will be utilised for improving the 
working of the Railways.  Then, they will have  to less depend on ticket fares and 
other things to run the Railways.” 
 
Land Management 
3.4.   All the Zonal Railways have been advised by the Railways Board in September, 
2001 to carve out their land management cells  as per their require ments and prevailing 
situation.  Land management cells have been carved out of the Engineering Department of the 
Zonal Railways.  The Cell is managed by an Senior Administrative Grade officer and 
supported by a Junior Administrative Grade officer along with Law Advisor and other 
supporting staff.  The Cell deals with the issue of land management, which include 
commercial licensing, prevention of encroachment s, maintenance of land records etc. and 
related court cases.  They also look after works not connected with land management. 
 
3.5. The Standing Committee on Railways have  consistently recommended in their 
Reports for setting up of a separate Rail Land Management Authority for proper management 
of land records, to prevent land encroachments, to get back the encroached lands to the 
Railways and commercial use of vacant land.  However, the Ministry of Railways have 
expressed their reservation towards the set ting up of such Land Management Authority 
instead the Ministry proposed  for setting up of Land Development Authority.  Substantiating 
their logic behind it, the Ministry of Railways stated. 
“The Railway is the owner of its land and its development rights alone will be 
transferred to RLDA.  This is necessary as transferring of vacant land having potential, 
would invite state taxation (running into huge amount) which otherwise is exempted 
for the Railway as per the constitutional provision.  The removal of encroachment 
from the Railway land is done under Public Premises (Eviction of unauthorised 

 18
occupation) Act  (PPE Act) 1971.  As per the provision of the Act, various notices to 
the encroachers are to be issued by the Estate Officers (they are nominated from  
within the Railway system through notification as per the Act) and served by 
custodian of the land which is Engineering Department on Indian Railways.  Inspector 
In-charge/Assistant Engineer in the Division is the custodian  of land in their 
jurisdiction, who draws the authority for eviction as per the Act.  Many a times the 
encraocher goes to the court against  estate officer’s order, which is to be fought by the 
Railway administration (custodian of the la nd).  Since RLDA will not be owner of the 
Railway land, initiating/processing/execution of eviction orders by RLDA will not be 
legally tenable.  Apart from this, Railway s have also been using Section 147 of the 
Railway Act-1989 for removal of soft encroa chments with the help  of RPF and local 
police directly, which cannot be done by RLDA  for the aforesaid reasons.  Further, 
4.23 lakhs hectares of Railway land spread across the country is being looked after by 
the cross  section of staff and officers (cus todian of the Railway land).  They are 
maintaining land boundary registers, land plan s, encroachment regi sters (duly signed 
by concerned departments responsible) et c. and initiate/carryout removal of 
encroachments.  They have to make regular  field visits to discharge other duties.  
During these field visits they inspect land position also.  RLDA will have to create a 
mammoth parallel organisation to deliver th e same.  Hence, entr usting the task of 
management/removal of encroachment was neither found legally tenable nor 
financially/organisationally prudent.  However, the encroachment of Railway land will 
be checked/prevented once it is put to alte rnative use by RLDA.  Also, RLDA will be 
associated in liaisoning with State Gove rnment for removing encroachments on such 
land which are identified for commercial development.  Focus of the activities, to be 
handled by RLDA will be generation of re venue through commercial development of 
land.”

3.7. The Railways follows the provision of  PPE  Act, 1971 in case of hard encroachments 
and Section 147 of Railways Act, 1989 for soft encroachments to get th eir land evicted from 
unauthorised occupation.  They also take prev entive steps to avoid further encroachment.  
Railways’ performance in removal of encroachme nts is being monitored in Board’s Office.  
Joint Procedure Orders have been issued by th e Zonal Railways to ensure better and effective 
coordination between various Departments includ ing Security Departments in dealing with 
encroachments.  Responsibilities  have been clearly defined in this Order and Railways have 
started making effective use of Section 147  of the Railways Act, 1989 to deal with 
encroachments.  RPF Rules have been amended to ensure active help from RPF in removal  of 
encroachments.  Railways’ performance in removal of encroachments is now being monitored 
in Board’s office.  Amendments to PPE Act 1971 have been proposed to equip the Estate 
Officers with enhanced powers in order to deal effectively with encroachers.  Ministry of 
Urban Development have forwarded the negative d ecision of the Ministry of Law & Justice.  
The matter has been referred again to Ministry of Urban Development with a copy to Ministry 
of Law & Justice for reconsideration.  This is under process.

C H A P T E R - IV 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
4.1 In the backdrop of the emphasis by the Planning Commission in Ninth Plan document 
for commercial utilisation of surplus land and the air space above such land to supplement the 
internal resources of the Railways, the latter started the process of identification, planning and 
development of such prospective lands to boost their non-tariff reve nues way back in 2001-
02.  However, due to some inherent constraints viz absence of clear-cut mandate in The 
Railways Act, 1989 empowering th e Railways to earn revenues by  developing surplus lands 
for commercial purpose, lack of adequate expertise in Railways about development of 
property, resistance by the State Governments for use of railway land other than the operation 
of trains, non-clearance of development scheme s on such railway lands by local authorities 
etc., the Railways could not ma ke much headway in this di rection.  To overcome these 
constraints, the Railways approached the Cabine t to get the mandate to develop the vacant 
land for commercial purposes and th e Cabinet approved the same on 8
th December, 2004.  In 
pursuance to that, the Ministry introduced The Railways (Amendment) Bill, 2004 in Rajya 
Sabha in December, 2004 during the Third Session of Parliament (14 th Lok Sabha) to get 
legislative sanction to develop surplus lands and air space above such lands for commercial 
purpose. 
  
 The proposed Bill envisages the establishm ent of a Rail Land Development Authority 
by amending the existing Railw ays Act, 1989 to exclusively d eal with the development of 
surplus land lying with  Railways and not required at least for next 15-20 years for railway 
operations. 
 
4.2  The Committee heard the view s of the representatives of  the Ministry of Railways 
and the Ministry of Law & Justice on the Bill so  as to form a balanced  view on the subject.  
After in depth deliberations, the Committee came to the conclusion that development of 
surplus land for commercial purpose does not violat e the sanctity of the mandate given to the 
Railways, rather it supplements the railways re venue which can help th e Railways to provide 
better passenger amenities to the railway commuters.  
 
4.3 The Bill seeks to insert a new clause, name ly, clause 32A in Section 2 of the Railway 
Act, 1989 for the purpose of defining the term ‘railway land’.  This clause defines the railway 

 21
land as “any railway land other than falling unde r the railway track”.  This is a clumsily 
worded definition which can only create confusi on.  Apart from the gl aring grammatical and 
structural error it contains, this definition does not  in fact define the railway land.  The word 
‘any railway land’ do not constitute a precise definition of railway land. 
 
 The Committee note that Section 2 (31) of the Railway Act, 1989 contains the 
definition of the term ‘railway’ which includes the railway land also.  Sub-clause (a) of 
Clause 31 says that Railway includes ‘all la nds within the fences or other boundary marks 
indicating the limits of the land appurtenant to a railway’.   
 
 The Committee feel that this  definition of railway land is correct, comprehensive and 
unambiguous and therefore a separate definition of this term is not necessary.  Further to give 
a definition of the same term at two places in the same Section is a example of poor  
draftsmanship.  The Committee, therefore, suggest that Clau se 32A should adopt the same 
definition of land as is given in Clause 31(a) of the Railway Act.   
 
4.4 Clause 4B of the Bill deals with th e composition of the proposed Railway Land 
Development Authority.  As per Clause 4B(1) the Authority shall c onsist of a Chairman, 
Vice-Chairman and not more than  four members including expe rt from outside the railway 
administration.  The Committee  have been informed that the expert on the panel should have  
expertise in real estate planning and development.    However, Clause 4B(3) states ‘The Vice-
Chairman and the other members shall be appoint ed by the Central Government and shall be 
chosen from amongst persons who are or have been workin g in the Civil Engineering, 
Finance and Traffic disciplines of   railway administration and ha ving adequate experience in 
the relevant discipline as the Central Governme nt may consider necessary.’ This would mean 
that the Vice Chairman and all the other members would be drawn from the different 
disciplines of the Railway,  wh ereas Clause 4B(1) of  the Bill suggest that one of the four 
members will be an expert from outside the Railways.  The expert from outside the Railway is 
being brought in mainly to deal with the deve lopment of land for which no expertise is 
available in the Railways.     The Committee find that both the Clauses  are thus contradictory 
to each other. They r ecommend that the Sub Clause(1) an d (3) of the Clause 4B of the 
Railways (Amendment) Bill, 2004 be revised and redrafted in order to remove the glaring 
contradiction before the Bill is placed in Parliament for adoption.   
 

 22
4.5 Regarding the functions of the Railway La nd Development Author ity in the Bill, the 
Committee observe that in Clause  4D(1), 4D2(ii) and 4D2(iv) it has been respectively stated 
that the Authority shall discharge such f unctions/exercise such powers of the Central 
Government or a railway administration , to develop railway land for commercial use as may 
be entrusted by the Central Government or a railway administration and to carry out any other 
work or function as may be entrusted to it by the Central Gove rnment or a railway 
administration.  The words “railway administration” used in the Clause are redundant because 
the railway administration is subsumed in the term  the Central Government.  The Central 
Government is the authority which creates this body and vests the duties and functions in it.  
Further the words ‘a railway administration’ used  in this Clause are inappropriate. Under the 
Railway Act, 1989 ‘railway admi nistration’ is defined as General Manager of the Zonal 
Railways. The Rail Land Deve lopment Authority is a higher authority with the Member 
Engineering of the Railway Board  as its Chairman and it is quite  inappropriate to say that it 
will exercise the powers and f unctions of the General Manager of a Zonal Railway which is a 
lower authority.   
 
 The Committee, therefore, recommend that  the words ‘a  railw ay administration’ 
should be deleted from Clause 4D(1) and 4D(2) (ii) and (iv).    
 
 
4.6 In the course of examination of the propos ed Bill, the Committee came across the fact 
that some States provided land to the Railway s free of cost for laying railway lines, 
establishing production units  and other operati onal requirements etc. in their respective 
States.  A part of such lands is still lying unused or not required for operational purposes in 
the foreseeable future.  The Committee are of the view that such lands, if identified as surplus, 
may not be utilised for commerc ial purpose  and be considered  for returning it to the 
concerned States for some public use such as roads, construction of buildings for public utility 
etc. 

 23
 
 4.7  While preparing the schemes for develo pment of railway land, the Railways should 
take a humanitarian view of settlement colonies  that have existed for over 50-60 years.  In 
case of vendors operating on the railway land close to tracks for long ti me, Government may, 
after developing such lands, consider providing them space therein on a reasonable rent.
